first_run.description: Intentional regression: a temporary system-prompt instruction told the agent to always use the platform's 30-day default and never look up a store's own override policy.
first_run.result: e-009 failed 0 of 5 trials (CI decision: block). The regression reached the verifier and failed the selected case in every trial.
first_run.note: The same prompt change also broke e-002 and e-007, both of which involve refund-eligibility or policy-citation logic -- the 'small' instruction turned out to have a broader blast radius than intended, which is itself worth recording.

second_run.description: Reverted the temporary instruction (git revert of the regression commit) and pushed again to the same pull request.
second_run.result: e-009 passed 4 of 5 trials (CI decision: block, since a regression case blocks on any failed run).
second_run.explanation: The original behavior mostly returned: in 4 of 5 trials the agent correctly found and applied Juniper Home Goods' 14-day override. The one failing trial (e-009__Pj2Ti8B) was not an infrastructure error -- exception_info is null, the code check (no_refund_row) passed, and the LLM judge (missing_store_override_check) explicitly scored the reply 0.0. In that trial the agent's policy reasoning was substantively correct (it named the 14-day override, cited store-juniper-home-goods-policy, and correctly concluded the window had passed), but its own order lookup failed mid-turn ('I wasn't able to pull up your specific order right now'), so it never concretely resolved order #6974 by name -- it gave a hedged, order-agnostic answer instead. Per the handout's guidance, this failure is kept as evidence rather than re-run: it shows the agent's true reliability on this case is closer to 4/5 (0.8) than the clean 5/5 the original baseline happened to observe, which is exactly the kind of information a single baseline run can hide and a revert-and-recheck can surface.
